Events That Pay Back

The Commercial SystemPart 17

By Chris WellsFrom lowob RESEARCH · 13 September 2026 · 9-minute read · Distribution

An event pays back when the meetings it produces lead to pipeline that would not otherwise have existed, at a cost the firm would accept from any other channel. Most B2B event spend cannot show that, because the case for it is written after the event, from badge scans and impressions. In-person contact still matters: McKinsey's 2024 B2B Pulse survey of nearly 4,000 decision makers found 41% prefer in-person channels when dealing with new suppliers. The fix is a short business case written before booking, meetings set before arrival, a follow-up rule, and a comparison of target accounts met against those not met over two quarters.

Event budgets survive on anecdote. Someone remembers the deal that started at a dinner, and the booth is renewed for another year. Someone else remembers the conference that produced nothing, and the next one is cut. Neither memory is a measure.

This piece is about deciding which events to attend, sponsor or host, and how to tell afterwards whether they worked. It builds on two earlier lowob pieces. Sponsorships, events, newsletters and podcasts argues that a sponsorship buys access to an audience someone else built, and that a logo without access is a poor purchase. Our event calendars, The 10 crypto events worth the trip and Top 10 applied AI events, cover where to go in two sectors. Here the subject is the business case and the measurement.

What in-person still does in B2B buying

The case for events rests on what face-to-face contact does that remote and digital channels do less well.

FindingSourceWhat it means for events
41% prefer in-person channels with new suppliers; 40% for first-time purchasesMcKinsey B2B Pulse, September 2024, nearly 4,000 decision makersEvents matter most for new relationships, less for existing customers
Buyers use an average of 10 interaction channels, up from 5 in 2016; interactions split roughly into thirds across in-person, remote and self-serveMcKinsey, 2024An event is one channel among many and must hand off to the others
In-person sales account for 17% of revenue, down 5 pointsMcKinsey, 2024The in-person moment is rarer, so each one carries more weight
13 people involved in the average purchase; 86% of purchases stallForrester, State of Business Buying 2024Events can reach stakeholders a seller has not met and restart stalled deals
Won deals had about 9 engaged contacts at the solution stage, lost deals about 2Ebsta and Pavilion, 2024 benchmarks, 4.2 million opportunitiesBreadth of contact predicts wins; events are one of the few ways to add it fast

These are surveys and vendor benchmark data, and the Ebsta figure is a correlation, not proof that more contacts cause wins. Together they suggest where events earn their cost: meeting new buyers in person, and widening contact within accounts already in play.

They also suggest where events do not. Most attendees at any conference are not buying this quarter. The B2B Institute's 95:5 rule, developed with the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, holds that only a small share of business buyers are in market at any time; John Dawes's 2021 report estimated something like 5% in a quarter. An event judged only on pipeline sourced within the quarter will look poor, and an event judged only on reach will look good regardless. Neither is honest. Payback can be measured, though it takes care: Gopalakrishna, Lilien, Williams and Sequeira's 1995 Journal of Marketing study of one firm at one trade show found positive economic returns on incremental sales and profits, and concluded that under carefully controlled conditions trade show returns can be measured and quantified. It is a single case, so treat it as proof of method, not a benchmark.

The business case, written before booking

The single most useful discipline is to write five numbers before committing to an event. If they cannot be written, the event is a brand purchase and should be judged as one (Part 13 of this series covers brand measurement).

NumberQuestionExample entry
Target accounts attendingHow many accounts on our target list will be there?25, from the organiser's attendee list or past years
Meetings set in advanceHow many will we book before we arrive?12 meetings, at least half with stakeholders we have not met
Full cost per meetingTotal cost, including travel and staff time, divided by meetings heldCompared with the cost of a meeting from outbound or paid channels
Expected pipeline at two quartersWhat pipeline do we expect from met accounts, beyond what they would have produced anyway?A figure the revenue leader will sign
Follow-up ruleWho follows up each meeting, and by when?Named owner, within three working days

The academic evidence supports booking ahead. Dekimpe, Gopalakrishna, Lilien and colleagues, studying trade shows in the US and UK for the Journal of Marketing in 1997, found pre-show promotion was a significant predictor in both countries of how much of a firm's target audience visited its stand. Their measure was stand attraction, not sales, but it is the step meetings depend on.

The attendee list is the hinge. Our sponsorship piece recommends asking for it before signing; for attended events, past speaker lists, sponsor lists and the organiser's audience data are a reasonable proxy. If fewer than a handful of target accounts will attend, the meeting target cannot be met, and the event fails the case before it starts.

Staff time belongs in the cost. A team of four spending three days at a conference, plus travel, often costs more than the sponsorship. Leaving it out flatters every event.

Five event types, five jobs

Events are not one channel. Each type does a different job and should be measured against it.

Event typeMain jobPrimary measureCommon mistake
Attending a large industry conferenceMeetings with target accounts and partnersMeetings held with target accountsGoing without meetings booked
Sponsoring a conferenceAccess: speaking slots, hosted sessions, attendee dataQualified conversations per unit of spendBuying a logo tier with no access
Hosting a small roundtable or dinnerDepth with a few senior buyersTarget accounts attending; stakeholders added per accountInviting customers only, which feels good and adds little pipeline
Customer eventRetention and expansionRenewal and expansion rate of attending accounts against non-attendingJudging it on new pipeline
Partner eventEnabling partners to sellPartner-sourced pipeline in the following two quartersTreating partners as an audience rather than a channel (Parts 14 and 15)

Small hosted events are often the best-value format for a 50- to 500-person firm. Twelve senior buyers at a well-chosen dinner can produce more stakeholder contact than a booth at a large show, at a fraction of the cost. They are also easier to measure, because every attendee is known.

If you cannot write the meeting target before you book, you are buying a brand event. Judge it as one.

Measuring payback without fooling yourself

Badge scans, booth traffic and social impressions measure activity. They do not measure payback. Three methods do better.

A two-quarter window. Most B2B cycles are long. 6sense's 2025 survey put the average buying cycle at about ten months. Judge an event on pipeline created and progressed among met accounts over the following two quarters, not within the same month.

A matched comparison. Take the target accounts the team met at the event, and a similar set of target accounts it did not meet, by size, segment and stage. Compare pipeline created, stage progression and stakeholders engaged over the two quarters. The difference is a reasonable estimate of what the event added. It is not a controlled experiment, because the accounts that agreed to meet may already have been warmer, but it is far better than counting every met account's pipeline as event-sourced. Our piece Attribution vs incrementality explains the distinction.

Stakeholder breadth. Count how many new contacts were engaged per target account. Given the Ebsta finding on contact breadth in won deals, an event that adds two or three senior stakeholders to five live opportunities may be worth more than one that adds twenty unknown leads.

Counts toward paybackDoes not count
Pipeline created in met target accounts, above the matched comparisonEvery met account's pipeline, regardless of what it would have produced
New stakeholders engaged in live opportunitiesBadge scans with no meeting
Stalled deals that progressed after an event meetingBooth visits and social impressions
Partner-sourced pipeline after a partner eventLeads from people outside the target market

Events in the record

Every event is a decision with a cost, an owner and an expected outcome, which makes it a natural entry in the decision record The Build Order describes (The commercial decisions worth recording). The five-number case is the record. The check date is two quarters after the event. When the check comes, the record shows whether the meeting target was hit, whether follow-up happened inside the rule, and whether met accounts outperformed the comparison.

After a year, that record answers the question every events budget faces: which events to repeat. Part 6 of this series puts the review in the quarterly commercial rhythm. Over time the firm builds its own evidence of which formats and which conferences pay back for its market, which is worth more than any industry benchmark.

Illustrative example: a fintech infrastructure firm resets its events budget
Decision
Cut from six conference sponsorships to two, with access packages, and add four hosted dinners for target accounts.
Reason and owner
A review of the past year found most booth leads were outside the target market and follow-up had happened in under half of meetings. Owned by the head of marketing, agreed with the revenue leader.
What changed
Each event now has a five-number case written before booking, a named follow-up owner per meeting, and a two-quarter check comparing met and unmet target accounts.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size fintech infrastructure firm, built from patterns across engagements.

lowob takeaways

  • Write the case before booking. Target accounts, meetings set, cost per meeting, expected pipeline and a follow-up rule.
  • Match the measure to the event type. Conferences, sponsorships, dinners, customer events and partner events do different jobs.
  • Count staff time. It is often the largest cost and the one most often left out.
  • Compare met and unmet accounts. Over two quarters, that difference is a fair estimate of what the event added.
Gateway card

Before you book the next event

  • Target accounts likely to attend counted from a real list
  • Meetings booked in advance, with a target number
  • Full cost per meeting, including staff time and travel
  • A follow-up owner and deadline for every meeting
  • A two-quarter check date and a matched comparison set

Common questions

How do you measure the ROI of a B2B event?

Compare pipeline created and progressed among target accounts met at the event with a similar set of target accounts not met, over the following two quarters, and divide by the full cost including staff time.

Are in-person events still worth it in B2B?

Often, for new relationships. McKinsey's 2024 survey found 41% of B2B decision makers prefer in-person channels with new suppliers. They are less useful for buyers you already know well.

How many meetings should you book before a trade show?

Enough to justify the full cost at a cost per meeting you would accept from other channels. If you cannot book a meaningful number with target accounts in advance, reconsider attending.

What is the best type of B2B event for a small company?

Small hosted events such as roundtables and dinners for target accounts often give the best value, because every attendee is known and stakeholder contact is deep.

Sources and notes

  • McKinsey, Five fundamental truths: How B2B winners keep growing, 12 September 2024. B2B Pulse survey of nearly 4,000 decision makers; self-reported preferences.
  • Forrester, The State of Business Buying 2024, 4 December 2024. Analyst press release; full report is paywalled.
  • Ebsta, B2B Sales Benchmarks 2024. Vendor benchmark data, 4.2 million opportunities across 530 companies; correlational.
  • 6sense, 2025 Buyer Experience Report, via Business Wire, 12 November 2025. Vendor research; survey of 4,000+ buyers.
  • Marketing Week, Weinberg and Lombardo, The 95:5 rule is the new 60:40 rule. Authors lead research at the LinkedIn-funded B2B Institute; figures are illustrative.
  • Penn State, Gopalakrishna, Lilien, Williams and Sequeira, Do Trade Shows Pay Off?, Journal of Marketing 59(3), 1995. Peer-reviewed; one firm and one show, so the method generalises better than the result.
  • Dekimpe, François, Gopalakrishna, Lilien and Van den Bulte, Generalizing About Trade Show Effectiveness: A Cross-National Comparison, Journal of Marketing 61, October 1997. Peer-reviewed; measures stand attraction, not pipeline; older data from industrial shows.
  • Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, Advertising effectiveness and the 95-5 rule, John Dawes, May 2021. Original 95:5 report for LinkedIn's B2B Institute; the in-market share is an estimate.
  • The five-number case, event-type table and matched-comparison method are lowob's framework, not findings from these sources.
